lesson.title: Two Protocols, One Internet: Living Through the IPv4 to IPv6 Transition
lesson.summary: Because IPv4 and IPv6 packets are not interoperable at the network layer, the transition between them has relied for decades on running both stacks side by side, tunneling one inside the other, and translating between them, rather than a single flag-day cutover.
lesson.body:
IPv4 and IPv6 were both covered as network-layer protocols, but it is worth being explicit about a fact that shapes everything in this final stretch of the unit: a device or router built to understand only IPv4 cannot parse an IPv6 packet, and vice versa, because the header formats, address lengths, and packet structures are simply different data on the wire. There was no possibility of a single global flag day where the entire internet switched from IPv4 to IPv6 simultaneously, given how many independently operated networks, devices, and pieces of software the internet is made of. Instead, the transition has been, and largely still is, a long period of deliberate coexistence, engineered through a small set of well-understood strategies.

The first and most straightforward strategy is dual stack, running both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously on the same device or router, each with its own address, so the device can communicate over either protocol depending on what the other end supports. This is covered in more depth in the next section, but it is worth noting here as the default, preferred approach wherever it is practical, because it requires no translation or encapsulation overhead: the device simply speaks whichever protocol matches its peer.

The second strategy is tunneling, encapsulating one protocol's packets inside the other so they can cross network segments that only support the outer protocol. A common example is encapsulating an IPv6 packet inside an IPv4 packet so it can traverse an IPv4-only network segment, emerging back into native IPv6 on the far side where a compatible router unwraps it. Tunneling, also covered in its own section next, lets isolated pockets of one protocol reach each other across infrastructure still running only the other, without requiring every router in between to be upgraded.

A third strategy, less central to this unit but worth naming for completeness, is protocol translation, exemplified by mechanisms like NAT64, which convert IPv6 packets into IPv4 packets and back at a translating gateway, allowing an IPv6-only client to reach an IPv4-only server, or the reverse, without either endpoint needing to support both protocols itself. Translation is generally considered a less elegant fallback compared to dual stack or tunneling, since it requires the translating device to rewrite addresses and sometimes payload data, and it can break protocols that embed IP addresses inside their application data.

None of these strategies is a permanent destination; each is a bridge intended to keep the internet fully connected while individual networks migrate to native IPv6 support at their own pace, driven by their own hardware refresh cycles, address needs, and operational priorities. Decades after IPv6 was standardized, IPv4 has not disappeared, which is exactly why dual stack and tunneling remain everyday, load-bearing techniques rather than historical footnotes, and why understanding both in detail, as the next two sections do, matters for anyone working with real production networks today.
